miniProject.title: A versioned framed key-value service with request identity, deadlines and a fault matrix
miniProject.brief: Put the service slice on the network: a TCP key-value service with a length-prefixed frame, a versioned payload, request IDs and trace context, deadline propagation and idempotent writes, running its work through the pool from the concurrency section. Then build a deterministic fault proxy and pass the full fault matrix with a verdict for every case.
steps: Define the wire format in kv/protocol.py: a 4-byte big-endian length followed by a UTF-8 JSON payload of at most 64 KiB, with a 30 s deadline for receiving a whole frame. The payload carries v (protocol version), id (request ID), op (put, get or delete), key, value, idem (an idempotency key for writes), deadline_ms (the caller's remaining budget) and traceparent. Write the framer as a pure function over a byte buffer and test it with two frames split at every offset, recv(5) reads, an oversized length, a zero length and a frame cut off by close.

Serve it with threads that only read frames and admit work: every decoded request goes into the WorkerPool, a full queue answers at once with an overloaded error, and each response echoes id and keeps the trace-id with a new parent-id. An unknown version gets a typed error naming the supported versions, and unknown payload fields are ignored so a newer client can still talk to an older server.

Propagate deadlines without comparing clocks across processes: the client sends its remaining budget, the server turns it into an absolute deadline on its own monotonic clock at arrival, and anything it calls gets only what remains. Check the AlgoMaster case in a test ([10,20,5] with bounds [80,100,10] gives [90,90,45]), and show with the proxy below that a 200 ms delay against a 100 ms client deadline gives a client timeout although the server did the work.

Make writes idempotent: an idempotency table keyed by (client, idem) holds IN_PROGRESS or DONE, the stored response and a hash of the request body. A duplicate of a DONE write replays the stored response, a duplicate during IN_PROGRESS never starts the effect again and gets an in-progress error the client may retry, and the same key with a different body is rejected. Client retries use capped exponential backoff with full jitter, only for errors the protocol marks retryable, and stop at the caller's deadline.

Write kv/client.py with a connection pool sized by Little's Law from your target rate and measured hold time (600 requests per second at 50 ms is 30 connections busy on average, so 30 leaves no headroom), a per-request deadline and request IDs generated by the client. Test pool exhaustion: a caller waiting for a connection gives up at its deadline instead of queuing forever.

Write a fault proxy between client and server driven by a schedule file: a seed plus, per connection and frame number, one action (pass, delay ms, drop request, drop response, duplicate, split into 1-byte writes, coalesce with the next frame, truncate and close, corrupt the length). It logs every action it takes, and the same schedule must produce a byte-identical action log on every run.

Pass the fault matrix: partial (1-byte writes), coalesced, oversized, malformed, timeout, duplicate, disconnect and server restart. For each case write a verdict row with the fault parameters, the client observation (result, error or timeout), the server state (applied writes and idempotency entries) and whether the effect is known applied, known not applied, unknown or safely repeated. Duplicated and retried writes must leave exactly one applied effect. State lives in memory until the next section, so keep the restart row as the open durability gap and rerun it there.

Capture one put with tcpdump -i lo (capturing needs root or CAP_NET_RAW), or run the server in a container and attach a netshoot container to its network namespace (--network container:NAME --cap-add NET_ADMIN --cap-add NET_RAW). Label the handshake, the length prefix, the payload bytes and the close, and keep the capture with the write-up.
deliverables: kv/protocol.py, kv/server.py and kv/client.py with framer, version, deadline, idempotency, retry and pool tests.
The fault proxy, its schedule format and action logs showing that a replayed schedule is byte-identical.
The fault matrix: eight cases with fault parameters, client observation, server state and verdict, and the restart row marked as the open durability gap.
One labeled packet capture of a put.

rubric.pass: The framer returns the same messages for every split offset and rejects oversized, zero-length and truncated frames with typed errors.
rubric.strong: A property test over random payloads and random splits backs the offset tests.

rubric.pass: Responses echo id and trace context, budgets shrink hop by hop on monotonic clocks, and expired work never starts.
rubric.strong: A test shows a request whose budget runs out in the queue is dropped by the pool, and the client sees a deadline error, not a late success.

rubric.pass: Duplicates of DONE writes replay, duplicates during IN_PROGRESS never start a second effect, and a reused key with a different body is rejected.
rubric.strong: Retries are jittered, stop at the deadline and back off on the overloaded error, and a seeded test counts the attempts.

rubric.pass: All eight cases have verdict rows, replayed schedules give byte-identical action logs, and duplicated or retried writes apply once.
rubric.strong: Every unknown outcome names the probe that would resolve it, such as a read by idempotency key.

miniProject.feedsInto: Capstone service slice: the versioned framed RPC, request identity, deadlines, retries and the deterministic network faults. Dossier: the fault matrix is part of its failure evidence.
